about: Topic map of the AP Precalculus Course and Exam Description (effective fall 2026), written in LevlPrep's own words from docs/apprecalc-research/framework.md. No CED text is reproduced. Every topic title is official (Course at a Glance); Unit 1 objectives and knowledge were read in the CED; Units 2-3 combine the official clarifications PDF with third-party summaries (source field); Unit 4 is a short outline (not assessed). Open points: docs/apprecalc-needs-author.md.

ced.title: AP Precalculus Course and Exam Description
ced.edition: Effective fall 2026, with the 2026-27 clarifications and corrections

skillNames.1.A: Solve equations and inequalities, with and without technology
skillNames.1.B: Rewrite expressions and functions in equivalent forms
skillNames.1.C: Build new functions by transformation, composition, inversion or regression

skillNames.2.A: Read information from graphs, tables, formulas and words

skillNames.3.A: Describe function characteristics as precisely as the representation allows
skillNames.3.B: Apply numerical results in a context
skillNames.3.C: Support conclusions with a rationale or data

practicesNote: Practice names and skills from the CED. Their MCQ weights could not be read, so mcqWeight is [0, 100] and nothing enforces them (practicesConfirmed false; needs-author practice-weights).

topics.title: Change in Tandem
objectives: Describe how the inputs and outputs of a function change together, from a table, a graph or words.
knowledge: A function gives each input exactly one output; the domain is the set of inputs, the range the set of outputs.
A function is increasing on an interval when larger inputs give larger outputs, decreasing when they give smaller ones.
Concave up means the rate of change is increasing; concave down means it is decreasing.
exclusions: Whether an endpoint belongs to an interval of increase or decrease (open or closed) is outside the course and exam.

topics.title: Rates of Change
objectives: Compare how fast a function changes at two points using average rates of change over small nearby intervals.
knowledge: The average rate of change over an interval is the change in output divided by the change in input.
A positive rate of change means input and output move the same way; a negative one, opposite ways.

topics.title: Rates of Change in Linear and Quadratic Functions
objectives: Find average rates of change of linear and quadratic functions and describe how those rates change.
knowledge: A linear function has a constant average rate of change.
For a quadratic, average rates over equal-length consecutive intervals change by a constant amount (constant second differences).
The average rate of change on [a, b] is the slope of the secant line through (a, f(a)) and (b, f(b)).
Increasing average rates of change mean the graph is concave up.

topics.title: Polynomial Functions and Rates of Change
objectives: Identify degree, leading term, extrema and points of inflection of a polynomial function.
knowledge: A polynomial of degree n has a leading term and a leading coefficient; a nonzero constant has degree 0.
A local maximum or minimum occurs where the function switches between increasing and decreasing, or at an included endpoint.
Between two distinct real zeros there is a local extremum; an even-degree polynomial has a global maximum or minimum.
A point of inflection is where the concavity changes.

topics.title: Polynomial Functions and Complex Zeros
objectives: Find zeros of a polynomial from its factors and describe their multiplicity and symmetry.
knowledge: A degree n polynomial has exactly n complex zeros counting multiplicity; non-real zeros come in conjugate pairs.
At a zero of even multiplicity the graph touches the x-axis without crossing it.
Equally spaced inputs whose nth differences are constant come from a degree n polynomial.
An even function is symmetric about the y-axis; an odd function about the origin.

topics.title: Polynomial Functions and End Behavior
objectives: Describe the end behavior of a polynomial in words and in limit notation.
knowledge: The sign and degree of the leading term decide the end behavior.
End behavior is written with limit notation as x goes to positive or negative infinity.

topics.title: Rational Functions and End Behavior
objectives: Describe the end behavior of a rational function from the quotient of the leading terms.
knowledge: When the leading terms divide to a constant, the graph has a horizontal asymptote at that value; when the denominator dominates, at y = 0.
When the quotient of leading terms is linear, the graph has a slant asymptote.

topics.title: Rational Functions and Zeros
objectives: Find the real zeros of a rational function and solve rational inequalities.
knowledge: The real zeros of a rational function are the zeros of its numerator that are in its domain.
Zeros and vertical asymptotes split the number line into intervals of one sign.

topics.title: Rational Functions and Vertical Asymptotes
objectives: Locate vertical asymptotes and describe the behavior near them with one-sided limits.
knowledge: A vertical asymptote occurs at a zero of the denominator whose multiplicity is greater than in the numerator.
One-sided limits describe how the outputs grow without bound near a vertical asymptote.

topics.title: Rational Functions and Holes
objectives: Locate holes in the graph of a rational function.
knowledge: A hole occurs where a zero of the numerator has multiplicity at least that of the same zero of the denominator.
The height of the hole is found with a limit.

topics.title: Equivalent Representations of Polynomial and Rational Expressions
objectives: Rewrite polynomial and rational expressions in the form that shows what is asked.
knowledge: Factored form shows zeros, intercepts, asymptotes and holes; standard form shows end behavior.
Polynomial long division writes dividend = divisor × quotient + remainder and finds slant asymptotes.
The binomial theorem, with Pascal's triangle, expands powers of a binomial.

topics.title: Transformations of Functions
objectives: Build and describe additive and multiplicative transformations of a function.
knowledge: g(x) = f(x) + k is a vertical translation; f(x + h) a horizontal one.
a f(x) is a vertical dilation (and a reflection when a < 0); f(bx) a horizontal dilation (and a reflection when b < 0).
Transformations change the domain and range in predictable ways.

topics.title: Function Model Selection and Assumption Articulation
objectives: Choose a function type for a context or data set and state the assumptions behind it.
knowledge: A constant rate of change suggests a linear model; rates that change linearly, or symmetric data with one extremum, a quadratic.
Area and volume contexts suggest quadratic and cubic models; n + 1 points determine a polynomial of degree n or less.
A model holds only on a domain and range that make sense in the context.

topics.title: Function Model Construction and Application
objectives: Build polynomial, piecewise and rational models from a context or data and use them to predict.
knowledge: Models can be built by transformations, from points, or by regression on a graphing calculator.
Inverse-proportion contexts (such as inverse-square laws) lead to rational models.
Predictions and rates from a model are stated with the units of the context.

topics.title: Change in Arithmetic and Geometric Sequences
objectives: Write and compare arithmetic and geometric sequences.
knowledge: A sequence is a function of the whole numbers; its graph is a set of separate points.
An arithmetic sequence adds a common difference: a_n = a_0 + dn. A geometric sequence multiplies by a common ratio: g_n = g_0 r^n.
Arithmetic sequences change by equal amounts; increasing geometric sequences by increasing amounts.

topics.title: Change in Linear and Exponential Functions
objectives: Tell linear and exponential functions apart from how their outputs change over equal input steps.
knowledge: Over equal input steps, a linear function adds a constant difference; an exponential function multiplies by a constant ratio (not 0 or 1).
An exponential function through a point with a known ratio can be written f(x) = y_i b^(x - x_i).

topics.title: Exponential Functions
objectives: Describe the graph, end behavior and features of exponential functions.
knowledge: f(x) = ab^x is always increasing or always decreasing, has one concavity, no extrema and no points of inflection.
An exponential function has a horizontal asymptote, described with limit notation.
The natural base e is about 2.718.

topics.title: Exponential Function Manipulation
objectives: Rewrite exponential expressions with the exponent rules.
knowledge: Product, power and negative exponent rules, and rational exponents as roots.
A horizontal translation of an exponential is a vertical dilation; a horizontal dilation is a change of base.

topics.title: Exponential Function Context and Data Modeling
objectives: Build exponential models from a ratio and an initial value, two points, or regression, and use them.
knowledge: The base is the growth factor; base minus 1 is the percent change per unit of input.
A model can be rewritten for another time unit (monthly from yearly).
Models predict outputs and find inputs within the domain the context allows.

topics.title: Competing Function Model Validation
objectives: Decide which of two models fits better using residuals.
knowledge: A residual is the predicted value minus the actual value (the course's convention).
A residual plot with no pattern suggests the model type is appropriate.
The size and sign of residuals tell whether a model over- or underestimates on an interval.

topics.title: Composition of Functions
objectives: Evaluate and build compositions of functions from formulas, tables and graphs.
knowledge: f(g(x)) applies g first, then f; composition is not commutative.
The domain of a composite needs the inner output to be in the outer domain.
The identity function leaves inputs unchanged; functions can be decomposed into simpler ones.

topics.title: Inverse Functions
objectives: Find and use inverse functions, restricting the domain when needed.
knowledge: A function has an inverse when it is one-to-one, or after its domain is restricted.
The inverse swaps inputs and outputs; its graph is the reflection over y = x.
f(f^-1(x)) = x and f^-1(f(x)) = x on the right domains.

topics.title: Logarithmic Expressions
objectives: Evaluate logarithms and use logarithmic scales.
knowledge: log_b c = a means b^a = c.
The common logarithm has base 10; the natural logarithm has base e.
A logarithmic scale shows quantities that vary by factors.

topics.title: Inverses of Exponential Functions
objectives: Use the inverse relationship between exponential and logarithmic functions.
knowledge: An exponential and a logarithmic function with the same base are inverses.
Adding to the input of an exponential multiplies its output; multiplying the input of a logarithm adds to its output.

topics.title: Logarithmic Functions
objectives: Describe the graph, domain and end behavior of logarithmic functions.
knowledge: f(x) = a log_b x has domain x > 0 and a vertical asymptote at x = 0.
It is always increasing or always decreasing, with one concavity and no extrema.
Behavior near the asymptote is described with one-sided limits.

topics.title: Logarithmic Function Manipulation
objectives: Rewrite logarithmic expressions with the product, quotient, power and change of base rules.
knowledge: Product, quotient and power rules for logarithms.
Change of base shows every logarithmic function is a vertical dilation of every other.
Each rule has a graphical meaning (a translation or a dilation).

topics.title: Exponential and Logarithmic Equations and Inequalities
objectives: Solve exponential and logarithmic equations and inequalities.
knowledge: Solve with the properties and the inverse relationship, and reject extraneous solutions.
Find inverses of transformed exponential and logarithmic functions.

topics.title: Logarithmic Function Context and Data Modeling
objectives: Build logarithmic models from points or regression and use them.
knowledge: A logarithmic model suits data where the input grows by a factor over equal output steps.
Models can come from two points or logarithmic regression.

topics.title: Semi-log Plots
objectives: Read and use semi-log plots.
knowledge: On a semi-log plot one axis is logarithmic; exponential data look linear with a log y-axis.
The slope and intercept of the line give the logarithms of b and a.

topics.title: Periodic Phenomena
objectives: Describe periodic behavior and build a graph from one cycle.
knowledge: A periodic function repeats; its period is the length of the smallest input interval that repeats.

topics.title: Sine, Cosine, and Tangent
objectives: Define sine, cosine and tangent from the unit circle, with angles in radians.
knowledge: A radian measure is arc length over radius; on the unit circle one radian subtends an arc of length 1.
Sine and cosine are the coordinates of the point on the unit circle; tangent is the slope of the terminal ray.

topics.title: Sine and Cosine Function Values
objectives: Find exact values of sine and cosine at multiples of pi/6 and pi/4.
knowledge: Exact values come from the special right triangles.
On a circle of radius r the point at angle theta is (r cos theta, r sin theta).

topics.title: Sine and Cosine Function Graphs
objectives: Build the graphs of sine and cosine by tracing the unit circle.
knowledge: Sine gives the vertical and cosine the horizontal displacement from the center; both oscillate between -1 and 1.

topics.title: Sinusoidal Functions
objectives: Describe amplitude, period, frequency and midline of a sinusoidal function.
knowledge: Amplitude, period, frequency (one over the period) and midline describe a sinusoid.
Sine is an odd function; cosine is even.

topics.title: Sinusoidal Function Transformations
objectives: Build and read a sin(b(theta + c)) + d and its cosine twin.
knowledge: Amplitude |a|, period 2pi/|b|, phase shift and midline y = d.
Cosine is sine shifted by pi/2.

topics.title: Sinusoidal Function Context and Data Modeling
objectives: Build sinusoidal models from a context or data and use them.
knowledge: A model comes from the maximum, minimum, cycle length and a landmark point, or from sinusoidal regression.
A model is valid on a domain the context allows.

topics.title: The Tangent Function
objectives: Describe the graph of tangent and its transformations.
knowledge: Tangent has period pi and vertical asymptotes where cosine is 0.

topics.title: Inverse Trigonometric Functions
objectives: Evaluate inverse sine, cosine and tangent with their restricted ranges.
knowledge: Inverse sine has range [-pi/2, pi/2], inverse cosine [0, pi], inverse tangent (-pi/2, pi/2).
The outputs are angles; sin^-1 x is not 1 / sin x.

topics.title: Trigonometric Equations and Inequalities
objectives: Solve trigonometric equations and inequalities on an interval or for all real numbers.
knowledge: Find the principal solution, then every solution in the interval using symmetry and periodicity.

topics.title: The Secant, Cosecant, and Cotangent Functions
objectives: Describe secant, cosecant and cotangent as reciprocals.
knowledge: Each is a reciprocal of sine, cosine or tangent, with vertical asymptotes at the zeros of the denominator.

topics.title: Equivalent Representations of Trigonometric Functions
objectives: Rewrite trigonometric expressions with the identities the course uses.
knowledge: The Pythagorean identity and its tangent-secant and cotangent-cosecant forms.
Sum and difference identities for sine and cosine, and double-angle identities.
exclusions: Half-angle identities and the tangent sum and difference identities are reported out of scope by a third party (not verified in the CED).

topics.title: Trigonometry and Polar Coordinates
objectives: Plot points in polar coordinates and convert to and from rectangular coordinates.
knowledge: A point is (r, theta); r may be negative and each point has many representations.
x = r cos theta, y = r sin theta and r^2 = x^2 + y^2.

topics.title: Polar Function Graphs
objectives: Graph r = f(theta) from the rectangular graph of r against theta.
knowledge: A change in input is a change of angle; a change in output is a signed change of radius.
Circles, roses, limaçons and cardioids.

topics.title: Rates of Change in Polar Functions
objectives: Describe how the distance from the origin changes on a polar graph.
knowledge: The distance from the origin increases where r is positive and increasing or negative and decreasing.
The average rate of change of r with respect to theta is a signed change in radius per radian.

units.title: Functions Involving Parameters, Vectors, and Matrices

topics.title: Parametric Functions
objectives: Describe a curve given by parametric functions.
knowledge: A parameter t gives each point (x(t), y(t)); the curve has a direction of travel.
topics.source: Course at a Glance titles; outline ours

topics.title: Parametric Functions Modeling Planar Motion
objectives: Model motion in the plane with parametric functions.
knowledge: Position at time t is (x(t), y(t)); x and y change separately.
topics.source: Course at a Glance titles; outline ours

topics.title: Parametric Functions and Rates of Change
objectives: Find rates of change of parametric functions.
knowledge: Average rates of change of x and y over a parameter interval, and the slope of the curve.
topics.source: Course at a Glance titles; outline ours

topics.title: Parametrically Defined Circles and Lines
objectives: Write parametric equations for circles and lines.
knowledge: A circle of radius r: (r cos t, r sin t); a line segment from one point to another.
topics.source: Course at a Glance titles; outline ours

topics.title: Implicitly Defined Functions
objectives: Describe curves defined by an equation in x and y.
knowledge: An equation in x and y may define a curve that is not a function of x.
topics.source: Course at a Glance titles; outline ours

topics.title: Conic Sections
objectives: Identify and describe parabolas, ellipses and hyperbolas from their equations.
knowledge: Parabolas, ellipses and hyperbolas as implicitly defined curves.
topics.source: Course at a Glance titles; outline ours

topics.title: Parametrization of Implicitly Defined Functions
objectives: Write parametric equations for implicitly defined curves.
knowledge: Conic sections can be parametrized with trigonometric functions.
topics.source: Course at a Glance titles; outline ours

topics.title: Vectors
objectives: Represent and combine vectors in the plane.
knowledge: A vector has magnitude and direction; components, sums, scalar multiples, the dot product and unit vectors.
topics.source: Course at a Glance titles; outline ours

topics.title: Vector-Valued Functions
objectives: Describe motion with vector-valued functions.
knowledge: A vector-valued function gives a position vector for each value of the parameter.
topics.source: Course at a Glance titles; outline ours

topics.title: Matrices
objectives: Add and multiply matrices.
knowledge: Matrix dimensions, sums and products.
topics.source: Course at a Glance titles; outline ours

topics.title: The Inverse and Determinant of a Matrix
objectives: Find the determinant and inverse of a 2 × 2 matrix.
knowledge: A 2 × 2 matrix has an inverse exactly when its determinant is not 0.
topics.source: Course at a Glance titles; outline ours

topics.title: Linear Transformations and Matrices
objectives: Represent linear transformations of the plane with matrices.
knowledge: A 2 × 2 matrix transforms vectors in the plane: rotations, dilations, reflections.
topics.source: Course at a Glance titles; outline ours

topics.title: Matrices as Functions
objectives: Compose and invert linear transformations with matrices.
knowledge: Composing transformations multiplies their matrices; an inverse matrix undoes a transformation.
topics.source: Course at a Glance titles; outline ours

topics.title: Matrices Modeling Contexts
objectives: Model changing states with transition matrices.
knowledge: A transition matrix predicts how a population moves between states over steps.
topics.source: Course at a Glance titles; outline ours

skillsTopics.title: Functions, Graphs and Notation
objectives: Read and use function notation, domains, ranges, intercepts and piecewise functions.
knowledge: f(x) names the output for input x.
Zeros are the x-intercepts of the graph.

skillsTopics.title: Interval Notation and Inequalities
objectives: Write sets of inputs in interval notation and solve linear inequalities.
knowledge: (a, b) leaves out its endpoints; [a, b] includes them.

skillsTopics.title: Lines, Slope and Linear Equations
objectives: Find slopes and write equations of lines.
knowledge: Slope is change in y over change in x; point-slope form is y - y_1 = m(x - x_1).

skillsTopics.title: Quadratics: Factoring and the Quadratic Formula
objectives: Factor quadratics, complete the square and use the quadratic formula.
knowledge: The vertex form shows the vertex; the discriminant counts the real zeros.

skillsTopics.title: Polynomial Arithmetic and Factoring
objectives: Add, multiply and factor polynomials.
knowledge: Common factors, grouping, difference of squares and sum or difference of cubes.

skillsTopics.title: Complex Numbers
objectives: Add, multiply and conjugate complex numbers.
knowledge: i squared is -1; a + bi and a - bi are conjugates.

skillsTopics.title: Rational Expressions
objectives: Simplify, add and divide rational expressions and find where they are undefined.
knowledge: A rational expression is undefined where its denominator is 0.

skillsTopics.title: Systems of Equations
objectives: Solve systems of two and three linear equations.
knowledge: Substitution, elimination, and a graphing calculator for the constants of a model.

skillsTopics.title: Exponent and Radical Rules
objectives: Use the exponent rules with integer and rational exponents.
knowledge: x^a x^b = x^(a+b), (x^a)^b = x^(ab), x^(-a) = 1/x^a, x^(1/n) is the nth root.

skillsTopics.title: Right-Triangle Trigonometry
objectives: Use sine, cosine and tangent as ratios of sides in a right triangle.
knowledge: Sine is opposite over hypotenuse, cosine adjacent over hypotenuse, tangent opposite over adjacent.

skillsTopics.title: Circles, Arcs and Special Triangles
objectives: Use the 30-60-90 and 45-45-90 triangles, arc length and the circle equation.
knowledge: In a 30-60-90 triangle the sides are in the ratio 1 : sqrt(3) : 2; in a 45-45-90, 1 : 1 : sqrt(2).

verified: All of Unit 4 is not assessed on the exam
1.1: open versus closed endpoints of intervals of increase or decrease
reported: 3.12: half-angle identities and the tangent sum and difference identities (third party, not verified)
language: Calculus wording such as "increasing at a decreasing rate" is not expected; say the rate of change is decreasing (2024 Chief Reader Report)
exclusionsSummary.unverified: Exclusion statements in Topics 2.2-3.15 could not be read; a person scans the CED for "outside the scope" (needs-author exclusions).

exam.delivery: Hybrid digital: multiple choice in Bluebook; free-response questions shown in Bluebook and handwritten in a paper booklet.
exam.calculator: Graphing calculator required in MCQ Part B and FRQ Part A, not allowed in the other parts (Bluebook has Desmos built in). Radian mode. Decimal answers correct to three places after the decimal point, rounded or truncated; never round partway.
exam.previousFormat: 2024-2026: MCQ Part A 28 in 80 min, Part B 12 in 40 min; each FRQ part 30 min.
